title: Redwood discovery - Eclipse Commerce - latency & throughput
summary: Discovery call to understand Eclipse Commerce's latency (p95) and throughput requirements for chat and short-completion use cases. Discussed target p95s (~300-400ms for short responses), concurrency (~50-100), streaming needs, and benchmarking approach. Customer leaning toward Dedicated for predictable throughput and VPC integration; asked for benchmark plan, pricing for Dedicated + hosted fallbacks, and security docs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Daniel Brooks (CTO, Eclipse), Priya Shah (ML Eng), Carlos Mendez (Infra)

Summary note (auto): Quick discovery focused on latency/throughput SLAs; customer interested in Dedicated for steady-state throughput and VPC options for security.

[00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we're excited to talk through your latency and throughput needs. Marcus is our solutions engineer — he'll handle the technical bits.
[00:15] Daniel Brooks: Thanks Sofia, yep thanks. We've got about 40 minutes, we want to make sure we cover p95 targets, concurrency expectations, and what you recommend for hosted vs dedicated.
[00:28] Marcus Lee: Great. Can you give us a quick baseline — what models and current infra are you using today for the chat assistant?
[00:34] Priya Shah: Sure — we run a mix of open weights internally, mostly Llama2 70B quantized on GPUs in our colo for production, but it's been a lot to manage. Latency is kind of all over. For short replies (~20-60 tokens) our p95 is around 700 to 900ms right now, sometimes worse if cold. We're aiming for p95 down to around 300-400ms.
[00:56] Carlos Mendez: And concurrency — we see bursts during sale events. Typical steady concurrency is 30 to 50 qps, but during peaks we need to handle up to ~120 concurrent streams. Also we do streaming to the browser — SSE — and want per-token latency to be low so UI feels snappy.
[01:20] Sofia Patel: Cool, that helps. So two separate things: short response p95 targets and sustained concurrency for throughput. For short completions, p95 300-400ms is ambitious but achievable depending on model size and where it's hosted. Dedicated capacity gives you more predictable p95s because you control the GPU pool and concurrency. Hosted can work if you accept occasional variance or if you use a smaller model variant for latency-critical paths.
[01:44] Marcus Lee: Yeah, exactly. A couple of factors: model architecture, quantization profile, sequence length, and whether you use KV/prefix caching. For example, if your prompts include a large shared system prompt, prefix caching can drop warm p95 significantly. Batching improves throughput but can add 50-200ms to tail latency if not tuned.
[02:10] Daniel Brooks: When you say 'prefix caching' — is that something Redwood manages automatically or we need to set up?
[02:16] Marcus Lee: Redwood handles prefix/KV caching in the serving runtime. You can configure which keys to cache and what TTL. In our Dedicated offering we also expose cache sizing and warmup options so you can pre-populate for predictable p95s.
[02:30] Priya Shah: For streaming specifically, are you emitting tokens immediately as generated or buffering? We want true token-by-token streaming, not chunked.
[02:37] Marcus Lee: We support streaming token-by-token over SSE or websocket. There are network and browser constraints that sometimes cause perceived chunking, but the runtime streams as available. You can also configure small micro-batches to balance throughput/latency.
[02:52] Carlos Mendez: Okay — what's the per-GPU token/sec ballpark we should expect? Our internal numbers on a V100-ish box are like 400-600 tokens/sec for the 70B quantized. We want to understand what Dedicated on modern hardware would give us.
[03:05] Marcus Lee: On current generation A100/H100-like instances with quantized weights and kernel optimizations, throughput can be in the 1k-2k tokens/sec range for similar models, depending on seq length. For smaller models or lower sequence lengths you can exceed that. But it's really workload-dependent — prompt length, output length, streaming overhead. We'll run token/sec benchmarks with your sample prompts to give concrete numbers.
[03:29] Daniel Brooks: Important for us: we care about cold vs warm p95. If a user hits a rarely-used product page the first request should still be tolerable. What's realistic for cold p95 vs warm?
[03:40] Marcus Lee: Cold p95 can be 2x-5x worse because of model loading and cache misses. Dedicated with pinned models and pre-warmed workers reduces cold p95 a lot. We typically recommend warm path SLOs for critical UX, and using a small fallback model for cold start. We can show numbers from our benchmarks.
[03:58] Sofia Patel: Also worth noting routing policies — you can route latency-sensitive requests to ded instances or to smaller, faster model variants. That gives you a good balance between cost and p95 SLOs.
[04:10] Priya Shah: On cost — we need the unit economics. Is Dedicated strictly flat monthly or are there egress/usage fees too?
[04:17] Sofia Patel: Dedicated has a reserved capacity fee for the GPUs and an optional usage overlay for bursts. Hosted has usage-based token pricing. Usually customers do Dedicated for steady throughput and keep hosted as a fallback for overflow — we'll include pricing scenarios in the deck.
[04:30] Carlos Mendez: Security question: we need VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for keys. Also audit logs for token-level requests. Do you support those in Private or Dedicated?
[04:40] Marcus Lee: Yes. Dedicated supports VPC peering and KMS integrations; Private (on-prem or VPC controlled) is where you get full customer control. We also emit audit logs and have retention controls. We'll share SOC2 docs and a security checklist.
[04:55] Daniel Brooks: Good. For the benchmark plan — what do you need from us to run representative tests?
[05:01] Marcus Lee: We'll need sample prompts (your top ~50 prompt+response shapes), typical sequence length distributions, concurrency profile (steady and peak), and any context that should be cached. We'll run three profiles: cold start, warm steady-state, and high-concurrency burst. We'll measure p50/p90/p95 p99, tokens/sec, and cost per 1M tokens for each profile.
[05:22] Priya Shah: We can share a sanitized prompt set. Our p95 targets are: 1) chat short answers (20-60 tokens) p95 <= 350ms; 2) medium completions (200-400 tokens) p95 <= 1.2s; 3) streaming conversational flow p95 per-token latency <= 100ms perceived. Are those realistic?
[05:43] Marcus Lee: Short answers at <=350ms is achievable on Dedicated with tuned quantization and pre-warmed workers for models up to ~13B easily; for 70B it's tougher but possible on H100-class nodes with careful tuning. Medium completions target 1.2s p95 is reasonable. Per-token perceived latency <=100ms depends a lot on network and client; we can get you close with micro-batching and streaming.
[06:05] Daniel Brooks: So sounds like tradeoffs: model size vs latency vs cost. We need throughput per device so we can capacity plan.
[06:12] Marcus Lee: Exactly. We'll provide a benchmark sheet that includes token/sec per GPU, expected concurrency per GPU at your p95 target, and cost estimates. For example, if a GPU can do 1.5k tokens/sec on your prompt mix and your average response is 150 tokens, that's ~10 responses/sec per GPU or ~600/minute. Then factor in concurrency and reserve headroom (~20-30%).
[06:35] Sofia Patel: Quick Q: are you using streaming as primary UX or batch responses?
[06:40] Daniel Brooks: Streaming primarily for chat in the web UI, but we have some async batch jobs for analytics that tolerate higher latency.
[06:48] Marcus Lee: Great. For streaming at scale, we also look at connection count limits — each open SSE constitutes a connection; Dedicated clusters can handle tens of thousands but you need load balancers and sticky routing. We'll include an infra checklist.
[07:02] Priya Shah: Another question — how does batching interact with streaming? I know batching increases throughput but streaming needs low latency.
[07:09] Marcus Lee: You can micro-batch at a very small size (2-4 requests) to preserve low latency while improving throughput. The runtime has continous batching that forms batches based on latency SLOs. If you set a hard per-request timeout of 100ms for dispatch, batching will only collect what's available in that window. There's always a tradeoff parameter you can tune.
[07:30] Daniel Brooks: For our benchmark, can you show both raw tokens/sec and user-experienced p95 with streaming enabled?
[07:35] Marcus Lee: Yep — we'll report both. We'll instrument client-side RTT and server-side generation latency.
[07:41] Sofia Patel: Okay, next — runbook for fallbacks. If Dedicated is saturated during big events, can we failover to Hosted transparently?
[07:49] Marcus Lee: Yes — smart routing supports fallbacks. You can route by policy: if Dedicated queue depth exceeds X or if p95 > Y, route to hosted variants automatically. There's also model-variant fallback (smaller model) for latency-critical paths.
[08:04] Carlos Mendez: How do you handle KV cache across replicas? If we have several workers for redundancy, cache coherence matters.
[08:10] Marcus Lee: Cache is local per worker for speed; we recommend sticky routing for sessions to maintain cache affinity. For global cache state you can use our external cache hooks but that's a tradeoff in latency.
[08:22] Priya Shah: For the benchmark scripts, do you support running locust/jmeter style clients, or do you provide a harness?
[08:28] Marcus Lee: We provide a benchmark harness that can replay prompt sets at specified concurrency and produce server+client metrics. We'll share it and a sample load script.
[08:38] Daniel Brooks: Ok good. One more thing — we need to log token counts for cost attribution. Does Redwood emit token accounting per request?
[08:45] Sofia Patel: Yes — token-level accounting and per-route cost breakdowns are in the console. You can export usage CSVs for billing.
[08:52] Daniel Brooks: Perfect. Anything else before we move to next steps?
[08:55] Sofia Patel: We'll recap the deliverables: benchmark plan + harness (Marcus), pricing and contract (Sofia), security docs (Marcus), and we expect Eclipse to share sanitized prompts and p95 goals (Daniel). We'll set the deep-dive next week.
[09:10] Daniel Brooks: Sounds good.

[09:25] (follow-up Q&A, shorter exchanges and clarifications)
[12:00] Priya Shah: One nit — for streaming, do you support function calling that emits structured JSON mid-stream? We rely on that to call downstream services as tokens arrive.
[12:10] Marcus Lee: We support function/tool calling patterns and structured outputs; streaming structured chunks is supported but you need to handle partial JSON reassembly on the client. We have SDK helpers for that.
[12:25] Carlos Mendez: During our peaks we want autoscale to be fast — what's the typical spin-up time for additional workers in Dedicated?
[12:32] Marcus Lee: With warm pools configured, we can have workers ready in a few seconds to <60s. Cold spin-up (provisioning new instances) depends on infra but we recommend warm capacity for tight SLOs.
[12:45] Daniel Brooks: Great. Anything else on security? Priya: no, we just need the checklist and SOC2.
[12:51] Sofia Patel: We'll attach those in the follow-up.

[13:10] Closing recap by Sofia: Action items and next steps as discussed. We'll aim to send the benchmark plan by Monday and schedule the technical deep-dive for next Thu. Thanks everyone.

[13:30] Daniel Brooks: Thanks, appreciate it.

(Transcript end)
